blocking.section: §5.3 adjoint table; §11 generated order; §11.1 inverse/K28 and bound ref adj recipe

steps.claim: The scheduled generated order is fixed above gate level. The adjoint table replaces qinplace @G @H by qinplace @H @G; each such instruction explicitly generates allocation t, allocation f, first oracle, exchange, second oracle, release t, release f, in that order. K28 preserves this instruction-defined sequence.

The newly bound catalog also prescribes a different construction of an action adjoint: recipe adj(B) is exactly inverse(splice B). §11.1 defines inverse as reversal of the fully expanded leaves, swapping allocation/release, and K28 says the inverse traversal retains the original ordinals. There is no stated precedence separating this recipe from the source adjoint table.
steps.by: clause:ISA-11.1-P5.S9; clause:ISA-11.1-P31.S4; witness:spec/ref-0.9-draft.json recipe kind="adj", body=[{"inverse":true,"body":[{"splice":"B"}]}], bound by ISA-11.1-P39.S2

steps.claim: Take an action consisting of one certified qinplace, n=1, F=4, with identity inverse-pair oracles. At its private-operation level the source-table adjoint is alloc t[1](0), alloc f[4](1), call H, swap(2), call G, release t(3), release f(4). The catalog leaf inverse instead is alloc f[4](4), alloc t[1](3), call H-adjoint, swap(2), call G-adjoint, release f(1), release t(0). Oracle involution makes the interface results equal but does not make these traces or allocation ordinals equal. Callee-local events have their separate ordinal spaces and do not remove this difference.
steps.by: witness:reverse([(alloc t[1],0),(alloc f[4],1),(call G,G-local),(swap x t,2),(call H,H-local),(release t,3),(release f,4)]) and exchange alloc/release; clause:ISA-11.1-P29; clause:ISA-11.1-P31.S1; step:<1>1; step:<1>2

steps.claim: For example, a matching alloc decision at generated=0 assigns a class to private t under the source-table trace, but matches no private allocation in the leaf-inverse trace (ordinal 0 is a release there). Thus the same scheduled call has different resolved private-frame classes and potentially different class resource charges. This is an S0 contract contradiction, not a claim that either circuit implements the wrong bijection.

blocking.fix: In §5.3/§11.1 explicitly choose the canonical scheduled action-adjoint expansion. I would preserve the instruction-table rule and K28: state, "Before ref recipe instantiation, form an action adjoint by the §5.3 instruction replacements. In particular adj(qinplace G H) instantiates qinplace H G with private allocations t then f, releases t then f, and its own instruction ordinal space. Raw inverse constructors used to reverse an already expanded machine row retain the forward ordinals; they are not a substitute for this source qinplace adjoint rule. The qif replacement still reverses its complete §4.6 expansion, including lifetimes." Change the catalog adj adapter so it consumes the source-adjointed body rather than blindly leaf-inverting every source operation, and update the bound library hash wherever used. The corrected private trace for n=1/F=4 is alloc t[1](0), alloc f[4](1), H, swap(2), G, release t(3), release f(4). A second viable resolution is to make the table only an extensional identity and explicitly require scheduled adjoints to use the literal leaf inverse, with trace alloc f[4](4), alloc t[1](3), H-adjoint, swap(2), G-adjoint, release f(1), release t(0); that alternative must expressly delimit the above-gate-order/K28 rules. Either resolution must say which trace a scheduler, executor and estimator share, and add the missing dependencies on ISA-5.3-P4, ISA-11-P2 and ISA-11.1-P29.

steps.claim: For a one-bit qcopy cleanup, reverse can be a CX followed by release, while recompute first creates fresh scratch, computes a copy, XORs it, uncomputes and releases it. Selecting cleanup by its first emitted leaf would therefore use a carrier changed by the selection itself; selecting independently on all leaves can assign conflicting realisations to one cleanup.
